docs.title: Course work for 113475 Software Defined Infrastructure
docs.text: This documentation is meant to supplement the submitted code for the Software defined Infrastructure lecture exercises.

docs.title: Exercise solutions
docs.text:
All solutions are documented and can be navigated to via the sidebar to the left. There is a page for each exercise, containing entries which detail the exercise description, document the implemented solution, and a verification of the intended results.

Before viewing the solutions, it is advisable to read through the 0. Preliminaries section. It details some information about used commands, the environment the solutions were implemented in, etc.

The documentation has been written as documentation of results, but in a manner that can be followed along to reproduce said results. If exercises build on each other, previous solution approaches are presumed to be known and won't be rehashed in detail for each individual documentation.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
To follow the solutions provided, please ensure the following prerequisites are met:

  • Generating SSH Key-Pair
  • Install Terraform
  • Hetzner Signup
  • Generating an API Token

docs.title: Aliases
docs.text: To facilitate more efficient interaction with the CLI tools used when creating cloud infrastructure, some aliases have been created. These are documented here in case they show up in screenshots of the conducted steps:

docs.title: SSHDM
docs.text:
alias sshdm="ssh -i ~/.ssh/hdm"

The public / private key-pair hdm was used during the exercise period. Since multiple key-pairs were available on the host system, an alias was created to make connecting to the Hetzner instances easier.

docs.title: VCI
docs.text:
alias vci='check-jsonschema --schemafile https://raw.githubusercontent.com/canonical/cloud-init/main/cloudinit/config/schemas/schema-cloud-config-v1.json'

Short for validate cloud-init, this alias was used to shorten the call to a third-party validation utility. Since the cloud-init package is not available for the system used during course work, the official JSON schema by Canonical was used to validate yaml configurations via check-jsonschema.

docs.title: .env.template
docs.text:
This template contains the environment variables which are used throughout all solutions. Copy the template and change the contents to contain your secrets. Rename the file to .env and source it to reproduce the documented results.

To learn more, visit:

  • Dotenv
  • The Linux Documentation Project - Sourcing a file

docs.title: Apply script
docs.text:
A script to prepare the shell and call terraform apply lays in the Terraform directory:

.
├── README.md
├── mkdocs
└── Terraform
    ├── apply.sh
    └── ...

It can be called with any exercise number as a command line argument. The script will source the .env file in the directory of the provided exercise number and call both terraform init and terraform apply from inside the directory.

The script was written to make the exercise results easily reproducible from the course work home directory.

docs.title: Task
docs.text: No. 19 Cloud-init for starters

docs.title: Cloud-init for starters
docs.text: Follow Hetzner's Cloud-init introduction and assemble a corresponding cloud-init script. Use the package_reboot_if_required: true directive in favor of an explicit reboot command. Use the Hetzner WEB Gui for manual server creation. Copy-paste your cloud-init script into the respective text field.

docs.title: Hetzner - Basic Cloud Config
docs.text: Summary of Hetzner's Cloud-init introduction.

docs.title: Step 1 - Insert first line
docs.text:
The cloud-init config uses YAML ("YAML Ain't Markup Language") as markup language. The file must start with a comment on the first line so that the code is interpreted as cloud-config by the server:

#cloud config

docs.title: Step 2 - Create user
docs.text: After the initial comment, let us start by creating a new admin user with sudo privileges and pre-configured SSH key.

docs.title: Step 3 - Update packages
docs.text: The first thing we do is an update of the package lists and installed packages. A fresh copy of Linux may have outdated packages with critical security vulnerabilities. In this step, you could install necessary packages for your projects too.

docs.title: Step 4 – Harden SSH
docs.text: We need to create a new file in sshd_config.d. Settings in /etc/ssh/sshd_config are automatically overwritten by any *.conf file within the sshd_config.d directory. - Deactivate the root login - Enable user for SSH - Change the default port for SSH - Deactivate password authentication - Automatic disconnection in case of incorrect login - Deactivate unused functions

docs.title: Step 5.1 - Configure fail2ban
docs.text: To secure the SSH network protocol, use fail2ban against brute force attacks

docs.title: Step 5.2 – Enable ufw
docs.text: Make sure you allow the respective SSH port.

docs.title: Step 6 – Create the server
docs.text: Open the Hetzner Console, select your project and create a server. In the "Cloud config" text box, enter the configuration you just created.

docs.title: Cloud-init configuration
docs.text:
To create the configuration, follow the instructions laid out in Hetzner - Basic Cloud Config. The page provides the full configuration necessary to create the basic server instance via cloud-init.

Cloud-init generates its own config file 50-cloud-init.conf automatically, which enables password login by default:

To ensure the desired SSH configuration takes effect, an additional parameter has to be added to prevent password login from being enabled:

ssh_pwauth: false

docs.title: Verifying the configuration
docs.text: To verify the configuration was created correctly, run the schema validation:

docs.title: Server creation
docs.text:
To create the server, log into the Hetzner Console, select a project, and navigate to the Servers tab in the sidebar.

There a server can be bought and created manually. Paste the cloud-init configuration in the Cloud config text box and buy the server.

Note: No SSH keys were provided manually, since the configuration will add them to authorized_keys automatically.

docs.title: Logging into the server
docs.text:
After waiting for the script to run, log into the newly created server. Since we changed the port SSH runs on, we have to specify -p 2222:

ssh -i ~/.ssh/hdm -p 2222 holu@167.233.84.111

Note that a login as user root is no longer possible:

Logging in has to be done as the user holu:

Attempting a login without a permitted public key fails without allowing password login:

Logging in was successful, confirming the cloud-init configuration was loaded. The specified SSH keys were placed into the server's authorized_keys file:

docs.title: Firewall
docs.text:
The configuration was supposed to set up a simple firewall, allowing only incoming SSH traffic to establish a connection.

The firewall created via cloud-init drops all packets except SSH traffic. ICMP is usually enabled by default if a server is created via the Hetzner GUI, but pinging the server for example doesn't work anymore since the firewall rules don't allow them through:

docs.title: Fail2Ban
docs.text:
In addition, fail2ban was set up. Repeated failed attempts are already penalized by the system, meaning fail2ban doesn't register the unsuccessful tries:

It is possible to confirm the tool was still set up by checking the file jail.local:

docs.title: Task
docs.text: No. 20 Cloud-init by Terraform

docs.title: Cloud-init by Terraform
docs.text: Re-use your Cloud-init script from Cloud-init for starters. This time follow Figure 1106, “Terraform triggering Cloud-init” using Terraform for executing Cloud-init rather than Hetzner's WEB GUI.

docs.title: Server creation with Terraform
docs.text:
To avoid having to create the server manually, server creation via Terraform was set up.

Run the following command in the directory 20. Cloud-init by Terraform or execute the apply.sh script with the command line argument 20 to create the server via Terraform.

terraform init && terraform apply

docs.title: Cloud provider
docs.text:
To be able to access the Hetzner API, the hcloud cloud provider needs to be initialized:

terraform {
  required_providers {
    hcloud = {
      source = "hetznercloud/hcloud"
    }
  }
  required_version = ">= 0.13"
}

docs.title: Hetzner Cloud API token
docs.text:
To be able to purchase a server instance, the generated API token (as per Prerequisites) has to be read from the shell environment:

provider "hcloud" {
token = var.hcloud_token
}

To be able to source the token from a confidential .env file, follow the instructions in the Templates preliminary. Alternatively, you can export the secret directly to be stored as an environment variable in your current shell session:

export TF_VAR_hcloud_token=YOUR_TOKEN_HERE

To learn more, visit: The Linux Documentation Project - Bash Variables

docs.title: Server creation
docs.text:
# Create the server
resource "hcloud_server" "g01" {
  name         = "g01"
  image        = var.serverImage
  server_type  = var.serverType
  location     = "nbg1"

  # Post server creation init script
  user_data    = file("cloud-init.yaml")
}

To read more about server resource creation, visit:

  • Terraform - Resources
  • Terraform Registry - hcloud_server

docs.title: Variables
docs.text:
Commonly used values have been stored in variables for ease of access:

variable "hcloud_token" {
  description = "Hetzner API token"
  type = string
  nullable = false
  sensitive = true
}

variable "serverImage" {
  description = "Server image"
  type = string
  nullable = true
  default = "debian-13"
}

variable "serverType" {
  description = "Server type"
  type = string
  nullable = true
  default = "cx23"
}

To learn more about Terraform variables, visit: Terraform - Variables

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
To be able to connect to the server immediately after the init-script has finished, an output directive was added in the file output.tf. It outputs the IPv4 address the server was assigned:

output "ip" {
  value = hcloud_server.g01.ipv4_address
}

To learn more about Terraform output, visit: Terraform - Output

docs.title: Result
docs.text:
The resulting server configuration was the same as described in Exercise 19. Results, except for the following:

  • A cheaper server type was selectable via the API, meaning the server ran on a machine with fewer resources.

Terraform allows creation of the server type Cost-Optimized CX23:

variable "serverType" {
  description = "Server type"
  type = string
  nullable = true
  default = "cx23"
}

Servers of type CX23 are only available in limited amounts and sometimes not selectable via the GUI:

  • The deployment was now possible via Terraform, meaning the need for manual GUI interaction was gone.

This means the deployment can be done via shell and therefore automated:

docs.text: No. 21 - Working on Cloud-init

docs.title: Working on Cloud-init
docs.text:
We continue our exercise series ??? by adding a Cloud-init configuration:

Follow Figure 1106, “Terraform triggering Cloud-init” and Figure 1106, “Terraform triggering Cloud-init” to create simple web server.

On success pointing your web browser of choice to http://<your server's IP> should result in something similar to:

I'm Nginx @ "95.217.154.104" created Sun May 5 06:58:37 PM UTC 2024

With respect to Figure 1112, “Watch out for your enemies!” inspect the output of journalctl -f on your own server for a while. Then modify your current sshd configuration:

  • Read the sshd_config(5) - Linux man page
  • Disallow ssh password based logins
  • Disallow root login altogether
  • Create a user devops eligible for both ssh login and sudo execution.

On success the following sequence should be possible:

$ ssh -v devops@95.217.154.104
...
debug1: SSH2_MSG_SERVICE_ACCEPT received
debug1: Authentications that can continue: publickey ❶
debug1: Next authentication method: publickey
...
Last login: Sun May  5 19:21:12 2024 from 217.245.243.187
devops@hello:~$ sudo su -
root@hello:~# hostname
hello
  • password is not among the list of allowed authentication methods.
  • User devops may execute sudo commands by virtue of his membership in group sudo.

On contrary ssh root login must be prohibited:

$ ssh root@95.217.154.104
root@95.217.154.104: Permission denied (publickey).
Read the cloud-init documentation and/or related tutorials to:

Currently, your (most likely outdated) cloud provider supplied distribution does not get upgraded on installation time:

$ ./bin/ssh
...
devops@hello:~$ sudo su -
root@hello:~# apt update
Hit:1 http://security.debian.org/debian-security bookworm-security InRelease
Hit:2 http://deb.debian.org/debian bookworm InRelease                                              
...
Reading package lists... Done
Building dependency tree... Done
Reading state information... Done
6 packages can be upgraded. Run 'apt list --upgradable' to see them.

# apt list --upgradable
Listing... Done
less/stable-security,stable-security 590-2.1~deb12u2 amd64 [upgradable from: 590-2]
libc-bin/stable-security,stable-security 2.36-9+deb12u7 amd64 [upgradable from: 2.36-9+deb12u6]
libc-l10n/stable-security,stable-security 2.36-9+deb12u7 all [upgradable from: 2.36-9+deb12u6]
libc6/stable-security,stable-security 2.36-9+deb12u7 amd64 [upgradable from: 2.36-9+deb12u6]
locales-all/stable-security,stable-security 2.36-9+deb12u7 amd64 [upgradable from: 2.36-9+deb12u6]
locales/stable-security,stable-security 2.36-9+deb12u7 all [upgradable from: 2.36-9+deb12u6]
Modify your Cloud-init configuration to upgrade your distribution at server creation time. If so required your system should also reboot.

  • Install and configure fail2ban, limiting ssh failed connection attempts.

  • Install the plocate file indexer package and initialize it.

On success all packages should be up to date:

$ ./bin/ssh
...
devops@hello:~$ sudo su -
root@hello:~# apt update
Hit:1 http://security.debian.org/debian-security bookworm-security InRelease
Hit:2 http://deb.debian.org/debian bookworm InRelease                                              
...
Reading package lists... Done
Building dependency tree... Done
Reading state information... Done
All packages are up to date.

Failed login attempts should be banned: Keep a second login open in advance when trying to simulate login failures! You should then see a report similar to:

root@hello:~# fail2ban-client status sshd
Status for the jail: sshd
|- Filter
|  |- Currently failed: 2
|  |- Total failed: 14
|  `- Journal matches:  _SYSTEMD_UNIT=sshd.service + _COMM=sshd
`- Actions
|- Currently banned:    2
|- Total banned:    2
`- Banned IP list:  170.64.133.30 213.136.94.219

Searching for file name components should work like e.g.:

root@hello:~# locate ssh_host
/etc/ssh/ssh_host_ed25519_key
/etc/ssh/ssh_host_ed25519_key.pub
